tagline: Summer estates, a former tent theatre and the Sandburg family’s farm.
intro: The Historic Flat Rock Scenic Byway threads a village of historic homes and forested landscapes south of Hendersonville. North Carolina DOT’s route includes 8.5 designated miles and a 2.9-mile connecting stretch, for an 11.4-mile drive taking 20 minutes. The department presents the byway through the village’s architecture, religious history and recreation, with St. John in the Wilderness, Flat Rock Playhouse and Connemara among its landmarks. The village takes its name from the granite rock formations scattered through the landscape.

Flat Rock’s summer community grew with the arrival of wealthy residents from the South Carolina Low Country. Charles and Susan Baring built Mountain Lodge in 1827, as the village acquired the name “Little Charleston of the Mountains.” Their private chapel became an Episcopal congregation. Another summer house, completed in 1839, became Connemara, where Carl and Lilian Sandburg moved in 1945. Flat Rock’s historic district includes estates with Gothic Revival, Second Empire and Stick Style houses.

Begin at Pinnacle Mountain Road and follow NC 225 north into Flat Rock. The playhouse and St. John in the Wilderness lie along this part of the journey. Turn onto Rutledge Drive, then Erkwood Drive. Kanuga Road supplies the connecting section before Little River Road returns to NC 225, with Connemara near the end.

moments.title: Flat Rock Playhouse
moments.text: Flat Rock Playhouse began its life on this site under a rented big-top tent in 1952. Robroy Farquhar’s Vagabond Players had already performed in a former grist mill at Highland Lake Camp. World War II interrupted their work when Farquhar was drafted; afterward, the troupe resumed in Tuxedo. The move to Flat Rock eventually gave them a permanent theatre, built in 1956 when they bought the property. Five years later, the North Carolina General Assembly named it the State Theatre of North Carolina. The playhouse is a professional nonprofit theatre presenting musicals, comedies and dramas.

moments.title: St. John in the Wilderness
moments.text: St. John in the Wilderness began as Charles and Susan Baring’s private chapel before they transferred it to the Episcopal Diocese of North Carolina. Bishop Levi Silliman Ives consecrated it on August 28, 1836, and twenty members formed a congregation. The first wedding held in the church united two enslaved people. The churchyard includes the burials of enslaved people and free Black people. For many years, the congregation was too small to keep the church open throughout the year; that changed in 1958. The building was renovated in 2004 and contributes to the Flat Rock Historic District.

moments.title: Connemara
moments.text: Lilian Sandburg was looking for a farm in a warmer climate for her dairy goats when the family found Connemara. They moved here in 1945. Carl spent his final twenty-two years on the farm and published more than a third of his work here. The house had been completed in 1839 for Christopher Memminger as a summer residence. The Sandburgs added bookshelves, new bathrooms and an indoor kitchen, turning the original kitchen building into a garage. The national historic site preserves the house, farm, pastures and mountainside woods. The interior is arranged to resemble the family’s home in the 1950s.
